pass_a_gloss: We stated that a soul of this sort, when found, must be seen as having natural goods forming its own world, by which God healed it, stored in its inner parts save for the high priest’s word, named its longings. Then the ancient foe, victorious in past conflict, troubled the soul fighting poorly for itself yet upheld by divine help, reached out via his power for evil, seized the governing faculty, and abandoned the God-forsaken soul barren of goodness. The peoples, per locality, symbolize the throng of sins that invaded the shaped ruling power, meant to be a vessel and true holiness of God for the clean mind seeking repose. God totally bars these peoples from entering the church; what could be more barred by God from entering a God-counted church-soul than flesh’s deeds and mindset, truly enemy nations to God? Since "flesh fights spirit," "flesh’s mind is hatred toward God," "it obeys not God’s law, nor can." They moaned from hunger and scant fare, the soul reversing and departing left the choicest things. How then did the named cravings, seized by foes, yield food-buying? But "the foe stretched his hand over all," and having filled himself with what he wanted, he abandoned the remainder, for which they procured sustenance. Jerusalem pleads: Lord, see my disgrace after famine ruined the world. Maybe varied cravings came first—those predicted, like what the foe had reached for—then each person’s own urges from the populace; shared stuff was seized, but instead of personal items, each purchased sustenance. Likewise, as Esau traded his birthright for red stew—earning the name Edom (Red Earth), becoming worldly by scorning birthrights and crafting earthly gains, which Jacob, as needful, received in a second account due to his bodily state—so Jerusalem acted. Yet God grants Jacob worth to claim what he’d wanted, even if unprioritized; Jerusalem’s folk gave themselves for food, not hallowing the act, but Babylonians poised to abuse the granted desires. Jacob knows how to enrich Esau’s goods; Babylonians misuse granted things for selfish ends. Thus the soul, lacking essentials, casts off heavenly lessons to the inquisitive seeking to learn for scorn and jeer. 30 He revealed the blaze atop the siege—either razing mighty structures or toppling the city’s elite—affecting soul and outsiders seeming to burn amid disasters. He also marks the seizure of the subjugated into slavery, as in a field entangled in nets. They failed to use freedom well. They forgot the past and didn't reach for the future, so they fell from honor to shame, from liberty to bondage, becoming dark and nameless through disgrace and arrogance; thus the city sinks into endless sorrow. Providence, he says, hasn't ignored my wickedness: God, as if seizing my sins, has woven them into acts of judgment through scrutiny. These things are to me like a yoke on my neck and a chain of servitude—just as I once served Babylon, my sins are that slavery, so I am powerless, handed over to forces I cannot resist. Soon after: his yoke rests on my neck. But this language shows we must interpret talk of our passions figuratively when speaking of God. How else could Jerusalem's sins be grasped as joined to God's hand, except as metaphor? No one takes this literally. How then is it not strange that Jerusalem is said to lift its neck metaphorically, yet God-related speech isn't heard the same way? We have set forth the proposition that when a soul of this kind happens to be encountered, it is necessary to recognize the natural good things belonging to it as a cosmos in its own right, through which it was healed by the divine, stored up in its inaccessible parts for everything except the word of the high priest, and called its desires. Moreover, upon all these things, the enemy who has gained mastery in the ancient contest, having afflicted the soul that wages war not well for itself but rather has been left behind worthily by divine aid, extends himself through the power of his activity into evil things, drags away the ruling faculty and leaves the soul that has departed from God desolate of good things. And the nations, according to the place, are to be understood allegorically as the crowd of vices that have entered into the formed ruling faculty, so as to be a receptacle and true sanctification of God for the pure mind wishing to rest again. These nations God utterly forbids from entering the church; for what else could we consider more forbidden by God from entering into a soul numbered in the church of God than the works and the mind of the flesh, which are truly nations hostile to God? For "the flesh wars against the spirit," "the mind of the flesh is enmity toward God"; "for to the law of God it is not subject, nor indeed can it be." They groaned because of famine and because of little food, the soul turning back and leaving behind provided the most precious things. But how did the previously mentioned desires, taken away by the enemies, provide for the purchase of food? Yet "the enemy stretched forth his hand against all things," and having been satisfied with taking what he wished, he left the rest behind, in exchange for which they bought food.

Jerusalem prays, Lord, look upon my shame, since you have destroyed the world by famine. Perhaps different desires preceded, first the foretold things which the enemy had stretched out his hand upon, secondly each person's own desires from among the people; and the common things were taken, but instead of the particular things, each one bought food for himself. Moreover, for guidance, just as Esau sold his birthright for red stew, of which he became surnamed (Edom meaning Red Earth; and indeed he became earthly, having despised the birthrights, having made earthly things which Jacob, as necessary, transferred to him in a second discourse because he happened to be in a body), so also Jerusalem. But the one who gives Jacob the worthy to obtain, which things he had desired, even if he did not previously choose them; but the people of Jerusalem have given indeed also themselves because of food, but not having sanctified this construction, but the Babylonians who were about to insult the given desires. For Jacob knows how to adorn the things from Esau, but the Babylonians do not use the given things for their own good. And so the soul, through lack of necessities, rejects the divine teachings to those who, out of curiosity, desire to learn for slander and mockery. 30 He has shown the one upon the conflagration of the strongest buildings touching or the fall of the superior ones in it of the city, to the soul and to those outside as if burning with the calamities. He also indicates the conception of those who have been subdued into slavery like in a field with nets,

Those who did not make good use of freedom. For these, "not stretching forward to the things that are ahead, but forgetting the things that are behind," they turned away from glory into dishonor, from freedom into slavery, and have become instead of honorable ones, darkened and obscure through dishonor and insolence; because of these things the city has fallen into endless grief. 31 Providence, he says, has not slept over my impious deeds; for God, as if taking them into his hands, has intertwined them through examination with the works of recompense. And these things have become to me like a yoke placed upon the neck and slavery imposed upon it; for just as I served slavery to Nebuchadnezzar, my sins are slavery, therefore I have become weak, delivered over to these things whose dominion I cannot withstand. And shortly after: His yoke upon my neck is shown. But it is indicated through the present expression that the things spoken of as concerning our passions ought to be taken more tropically in regard to God. For how otherwise could the impieties of Jerusalem be understood, joined to the hand of God, except tropically? For no one could speak these things literally. And how is it not absurd, that while the city of Jerusalem is said to lift up its neck tropically, the things spoken as concerning God do not hear the same manner?
